I was a schoolteacher for fifteen years before the conflict began. When the fighting first started, we were told it would end quickly. We were wrong. The first shell hit our neighborhood on a Tuesday morning in September. I remember because I was preparing lessons about the seasons for my youngest students. The explosion shook our building so violently that books fell from the shelves in my classroom. From that day forward, nothing was the same. We learned to identify different types of weapons by the sounds they made. My children would cover their ears during artillery barrages while I tried to maintain some semblance of normalcy for them. Our apartment sustained damage early in the conflict. The walls developed cracks, and water began seeping through the ceiling during rains. My husband spoke with neighbors who had already departed, collecting information about the route to the border. He told me stories of long walks through mountains, of nights spent sleeping in fields. streets that had once been familiar. The journey was exactly as difficult as we had been warned. We walked for seven days before reaching a refugee camp operated by international aid organizations.
